what: This is the Class B share of Rush Enterprises, which runs the largest network of commercial truck dealerships in North America. It sells new and used heavy and medium-duty trucks, mostly Peterbilt, and makes much of its money servicing them, selling parts and arranging financing and leasing.
customers: Trucking fleets, construction companies, municipalities and owner-operators who buy, lease and above all maintain commercial vehicles.
money: New and used Class 4 through Class 8 commercial vehicles.
Aftermarket parts and labour, the most profitable and most stable part.
Financing arrangement fees, insurance products and lease revenue.
moat: Trucks must be serviced where they operate, and Rush's dealership network means a fleet running nationwide can get a truck repaired almost anywhere under one account. Dealership franchise rights for a brand in a territory are exclusive and rarely available, so the network itself cannot be replicated.
risks: Truck sales are deeply cyclical and currently in a downturn: revenue fell from $7.9B in 2023 to $7.4B in 2025.
Freight rates determine whether fleets buy trucks, and freight has been in a prolonged soft patch.
Free cash flow of only $59.4M against net income of $276.6M reflects inventory and lease fleet investment absorbing cash.
Emissions regulation changes cause fleets to pull forward or delay orders, making demand lumpy and hard to plan for.
The Class B shares carry different voting rights from the Class A shares, and are less liquid.
opportunities: The parts and service business is far steadier than truck sales: trucks need maintenance whether or not new ones are being bought, which cushions the cycle.
The shares trade at about 0.88 times sales and 10.6 times EV/EBITDA.
Debt of $401.9M against $212.6M of cash is modest for a dealership group, much of it floor-plan financing on inventory.
A freight recovery would restart a replacement cycle that has been deferred for several years, and the average age of trucks on US roads has been rising.
watch: Parts and service revenue, which shows the underlying health of the business, and new truck orders, which show when the cycle turns.
